blocks.content: A ClusterRole is the cluster-scoped counterpart to a Role, either for granting permissions on cluster-scoped resources, or for defining a reusable permission set across many namespaces at once.
Where a Role is confined to one namespace, a ClusterRole exists at the cluster level, the same verb-and-resource structure covered in the Roles topic, just without the namespace boundary.

blocks.alt: The exact same permission structure, defined without a namespace boundary

blocks.content:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

code.content:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

codes.yaml:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

blocks.content: A ClusterRole serves two distinct purposes: granting permissions on genuinely cluster-scoped resources (Nodes, PersistentVolumes, both covered as cluster-scoped exceptions in earlier modules, a plain Role simply cannot reference these), or defining a reusable permission set meant to be applied across several namespaces without redefining it each time.

blocks.alt: Cluster-scoped resources, or a reusable permission template, two distinct real purposes

blocks.content: Here is a genuinely non-obvious detail worth knowing: a ClusterRole can still be bound to just one namespace, if you connect it with an ordinary RoleBinding (covered in the next topic) rather than a ClusterRoleBinding, only that one namespace actually gets the grant, even though the ClusterRole itself is defined cluster-wide.

blocks.alt: A cluster-wide definition, still scoped down to one namespace, depending on how it is bound

blocks.content: 4. The Broader Option, When You Need It
blocks.text: 4. The Broader Option, When You Need It

blocks.content: The practical rule of thumb: reach for a plain Role when permissions genuinely belong to just one namespace, reach for a ClusterRole when you need cluster-scoped resources, or want one reusable definition applied consistently in several places.

blocks.alt: A narrower, namespace-only tool versus a genuinely broader, more flexible option

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A ClusterRole is the cluster-scoped version of Role, needed for cluster-scoped resources like Nodes, or for defining one reusable permission set.
A subtle but important nuance: a ClusterRole bound with an ordinary RoleBinding only applies to that one namespace, despite being defined at the cluster level.
